fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Stillness, Wildness And Cleaning The Drawers", "body": "Eileen describes a stretch after a busy spring of keynotes when she chose to stop being busy, framing it with the idea that any waveform begins in stillness. She argues we are conditioned toward guilt-driven overdoing, that we have been raised in captivity for generations and lost touch with our wildness, and that health means getting back to it. Chance draws an I Ching card, \"Work on what has been spoiled,\" and Eileen answers with her motto, \"When in doubt, clean.\" She casts the home as an exploded view of the biofield, so clutter mirrors undigested emotion, and says clients often go home after a tuning and clear it out."}, {"title": "Why The Gut Knows Better Than The Head", "body": "Eileen says that until a couple of hundred years ago the center of consciousness was never placed in the brain, and she suspects widespread literacy pulled us up out of our bodies. She prefers keeping awareness in the solar plexus, treating the organs of digestion as a council rather than a single advisor: the heart can be childlike, the brain confused, but the gut knows. She calls the fixation on the pineal gland unnecessary. Her simplest route out of the thinking mind is listening, to birds, a brook or a single tuning fork, and she says an EEG once recorded her holding alpha for four minutes at a time."}, {"title": "Words Are Spells And I Am Statements", "body": "Asked how to call out negative self-talk tactfully, Eileen names \"I am\" statements as the biggest thing, since, in her view, by our word we create our life. She once said \"I'm fat, I'm broke, I'm sick\" herself, and now asks people to restate \"I am this\" as \"I have been this,\" which she says adds fluidity and lets the future differ. She argues we cannot berate ourselves into health any more than we could raise plants or pets that way. Chance says some people call self-loathing their only motivation, and that labels like \"I have anxiety\" have become a kind of social currency, especially among teenagers."}, {"title": "Untangling Hate And Choosing Appreciation", "body": "Eileen breaks hate into four feelings arriving together: powerlessness, anger, hurt and fear. She calls it valid but incoherent, and harmful to wellbeing if left alone. After moving to Burlington she caught herself hating cyclists, and by asking whether she was afraid, hurt or powerless she reached acceptance. Chance calls that the proper use of thinking, aimed at getting to the bottom of something. For people who insist they cannot choose how they feel, Eileen allows that some lows are genuine, then offers her favorite word, appreciation: gratitude pulls in, while appreciation extends energy outward. Chance adds that, like a house, whatever you appreciate grows in value."}, {"title": "The Electric Age And What Plasma Is", "body": "Asked about the turning of the ages, Eileen reads the symbol for Aquarius as electric waves and predicts medicine moving from a chemical, mechanical model toward frequency, saying sound healing went from unheard of to everywhere in her 25 years in the field. She says that while researching her master's thesis in 2010 she could barely find plasma in space in mainstream publications. Chance reads the Pisces symbol as regressive. Eileen defines plasma as the flow of electric charge, from the northern lights to lightning, and gives the definition of the biofield she says made her a renegade: the current flowing through the body plus the magnetic field around it."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Your words aren't just language; they're electric signals running through a biological system that responds to every "I am" statement you make about yourself. That's Eileen McKusick's framework, and this conversation takes it further than most interviews do, from the physics of what bioplasma actually is to the cosmological shift she believes will make frequency medicine the medicine of the emerging age.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: This is Eileen's second visit to InnerVerse, arriving on the back of her landmark book Electric Body, Electric Health. The conversation covers why productivity guilt is an ancient program embedded deeper than we realize; why the biofield is a fractal map of your home and your clutter; how Eileen trained her brain to hold alpha brainwave states for minutes at a time through the practice of deep listening; why she believes "I am" statements carry creative force at the cellular level; the precise difference between gratitude and appreciation and why one of them actually grows like currency; what bioplasma is and how she connects the aurora borealis and the Schumann Resonance to your body's electric field; and why she reads the Aquarian age symbol as electric waves.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Color, Loss And The Body That Does Not End", "body": "Eileen says the color someone wears can reflect, support or augment the color of their field, and that plenty of people stay stuck in one palette when an infinite one is available. She tells how a biofield tuning instructor named Claudia died suddenly during a Zoom meeting, how she felt Claudia's presence at her closet telling her to pick something bright, and how nearly everyone close to Claudia felt her show up in the three days after. From there she moves to the bioplasmic body, pure energy that cannot be created or destroyed, so a version of us lasts."}, {"title": "The Sonic Meridian Flush And Why Detox Feels Bad", "body": "Chance describes taking Eileen's work onto another show, where that host peeled off a sock on camera to demonstrate sliding the organ meridian points on his foot. Eileen answers that there is no end of ways to apply the slider and urges people to be little citizen scientists rather than defer to authority. She then walks through the sonic meridian flush, running weighted forks into meridian endpoints at the nail beds, face, legs and feet from both ends, and frames the detox that follows as garbage trucks finally reaching a neighborhood they had been skipping."}, {"title": "Widening The Lens On Habits, Food And Voice", "body": "Chance brings a case where someone clenched before every bite, traced back to painful orthodontics around age twelve and a later struggle with eating. Eileen names the remedy as stepping back and widening the lens until you can see where a pattern originated and choose differently, since default behavior only changes from a different perspective. The same principle carries into speech. She argues a monotone voice is your actual experience of yourself, and offers the kettle corn business she started in 2004 as the model, every handful different, which is how she varies tone and tempo in her books."}, {"title": "Splintered Selves, Hitchhikers And What Can Attach", "body": "Chance raises Tom Zinser's work on alter personalities and ego states, and Eileen separates two things people routinely confuse. Compartmentalized parts of a person, the Jekyll and Hyde anger nobody taught them to handle, are not the same as picking up a hitchhiker, and she says those come in many species, from things with humanoid faces to things like leeches. Her rule is that nothing attaches unless something is out of integrity to attach to, so a festering wound in the field draws whatever feeds on it, the way maggots mark a wound that needs cleaning."}, {"title": "Voltage, Shields And The World Pain Spot", "body": "Eileen ties resilience to artificial fields directly to voltage. When the inner battery runs low the shields drop, the outer boundary weakens, and foreign energies penetrate more easily, which is why some people cannot be anywhere near artificial electromagnetic fields at all. She notes the irony of cell tower signals scrambling our own cell to cell information flow. She also describes the world pain spot in the left armpit, first noticed the week after Robin Williams died when every client arrived lit up there, and says the medicine is people gathering to sing and dance instead of doom scrolling."}]
